papers.title: BTBD9-driven IMPDH2 ubiquitination governs sleep homeostasis by gating adenosine metabolism in the basal forebrain.
papers.abstract: BTB domain containing 9 (BTBD9) is among the most reproducible genetic risk factors for sleep-related disorders, yet its molecular function in sleep regulation remains unclear. Here, we aimed to define the downstream substrate, core brain region, and molecular mechanism through which BTBD9 regulates sleep-wake homeostasis. Population-scale genomic and brain expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) datasets were integrated to infer the direction of BTBD9-associated genetic risk in sleep-related traits. Basal forebrain-specific neuronal manipulation of Btbd9 was combined with electroencephalography/electromyography (EEG/EMG)-based sleep analysis and fiberphotomerty to define the relevant brain locus and functional output. Ubiquitinomics, protein interaction, ubiquitination, and enzymatic assays were used to identify BTBD9-regulated substrates and determine how BTBD9-dependent modification affects metabolic enzyme activity. Basal forebrain-specific genetic disruption, receptor pharmacology, and adeno-associated virus (AAV)-delivered interfering peptides were further applied to test pathway necessity and reversibility in vivo. human genetic analyses showed that BTBD9 variants associated with higher expression predicted a pro-arousal tendency. Consistently, neuron-specific deletion of Btbd9 in the mouse basal forebrain increased non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and extracellular adenosine levels. Mechanistically, IMPDH2, the rate-limiting enzyme in de novo purine biosynthesis, was identified as a substrate of the Cullin-RING E3 ubiquitin ligase 3 (CRL3)BTBD9 ubiquitin ligase. BTBD9-mediated ubiquitination at IMPDH2 lysine 195 (K195) relieved guanosine triphosphate (GTP)-dependent allosteric inhibition, thereby limiting adenosine accumulation and sleep pressure. Basal forebrain neuronal knockout of Impdh2 recapitulated the sleep-promoting effect of Btbd9 deletion, whereas adenosine A1 receptor (A1R) blockade attenuated this phenotype. AAV-delivered interfering peptides targeting the BTBD9-IMPDH2 interaction reduced IMPDH2 ubiquitination, elevated adenosine levels, increased NREM sleep, and rescued BTBD9 overexpression-induced abnormal wakefulness in vivo. These findings identify a BTBD9-IMPDH2-adenosine pathway that links human genetic risk to basal forebrain control of sleep homeostasis. By defining BTBD9 as a molecular regulator of purine metabolism, this study provides a mechanistic framework for understanding and potentially targeting BTBD9-related sleep dysregulation.

papers.title: Breathing-evoked potentials in humans during wakefulness and sleep.
papers.abstract: Breathing modulates cortical activities and cognitive functions, but the neurophysiological basis of the brain-breathing relationship is incompletely understood. We aimed to determine whether breathing at rest evokes scalp EEG-detectable potentials (as inspiratory occlusions do in the respiratory-related evoked potential model), whether these signatures persist during sleep and whether they are linked to sleep-organizing processes. We examined recordings from 729 participants in the Cleveland Family Study to identify cortical activity time-locked to inspiration during wakefulness and sleep, with a median of 7871 respiratory cycles analysed per participant. Breathing-related cortical responses were assessed in the time and frequency domains. Quiet breathing evoked a reproducible sequence of cortical potentials during wakefulness, including a pre-inspiratory component ∼300 ms before inspiration and several post-inspiratory peaks ≤3 s after. These responses persisted during non-rapid eye movement stages 2 and 3 (N2 and N3) and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, in which they showed simplified morphology resembling K-complexes and co-occurred with increased spindle-range activity. The pattern was present irrespective of body mass index and was qualitatively unchanged in the 203 participants free of sleep-disordered breathing, arguing against obesity or sleep apnoea as its origin. Scalp EEG can detect breathing-evoked potentials during quiet breathing in awake humans. These potentials persist during sleep with a morphology that resembles cortical activities previously associated with sleep stabilization. Further studies are needed to determine the physiological and clinical significance of these observations in health and disease. KEY POINTS: Spontaneous breathing at rest evokes reproducible breathing-related cortical potentials detectable with scalp EEG. These potentials persist during sleep. They are associated with time-locked modulation of cortical oscillatory activity.

papers.title: Diphenhydramine disrupts sleep architecture in 5XFAD Alzheimer's disease model and wild-type mice.
papers.abstract: Sleep disruption is common in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Diphenhydramine (DPH), a first-generation antihistamine with anticholinergic properties, is widely used as an over-the-counter sleep aid. We tested whether chronic DPH treatment alters sleep architecture in 5XFAD and wild-type female mice. Female 5XFAD (n = 16) and wild-type (WT) littermates (n = 14) were implanted with wireless telemetry recording devices to measure electroencephalography (EEG) and electromyography (EMG) continuously. After a 24h baseline recording at 5 months of age, mice received oral DPH (10 mg/kg) or vehicle at ZT0 for one month. After this chronic treatment, sleep was recorded continuously for 48h during ongoing dosing. Sleep was scored as rapid eye movement (REM), non-rapid eye movement (NREM) 1, NREM2, or wake. A survival curve analysis was used to investigate the microarchitecture of sleep phases after chronic diphenhydramine treatment. At baseline, 5XFAD female mice had more time in NREM1 than WT female controls and had shorter REM and NREM2 bouts. Chronic DPH treatment fragmented NREM2 in both genotypes, reducing long NREM2 bouts. DPH increased total duration of NREM1 and REM during the active phase, and disrupted the light-dark distribution of sleep. DPH did not rescue 5XFAD sleep deficits; instead, DPH treatment resulted in NREM2 fragmentation. Overall, chronic DPH use degrades sleep quality and increases fragmentation in both WT and AD-model female mice, which questions the use of sedating anticholinergics as sleep aids, especially in AD.

papers.title: A synchronized dual-scale platform combining flexible micro-ECoG and skull-screw EEG reveals frequency-dependent cortex-to-skull spectral gain in awake mice.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is the most scalable window onto brain dynamics, yet how cortical activity is transformed before reaching extracranial electrodes has largely been inferred from forward models rather than directly measured. We built a dual-scale sensing platform in awake mice that records a 16-channel flexible micro-electrocorticography (micro-ECoG) array and five skull-screw EEG electrodes on a single 30-kHz clock, enabling sample-aligned comparison of cortical and skull-level signals. Across 115 simultaneously recorded ECoG-EEG pairs from three mice, cortex-to-skull spectral gain was not frequency-flat but increased with frequency following a power law, indicating that skull EEG relatively preserves high-frequency cortical activity rather than acting as a simple low-pass copy. This gain was also non-stationary: it shifted across blocks of a fixed-order auditory protocol and was not explained by measured video motion, whereas trial-matched cross-scale coherence depended on the reference transform. With channel number equalized, micro-ECoG retained a larger unique spatial component than skull EEG. These results convert the cortex-to-skull relationship from a static modeling assumption into a measurable, frequency- and state-dependent quantity. For neural sensing, they provide an empirical calibration target for choosing electrode scale, reference, and analysis band and for validating EEG forward models and EEG-to-intracranial translation. More broadly, they indicate that noninvasive biomarkers and brain-computer interface features, particularly in high-frequency bands, should be interpreted through frequency- and state-aware cortex-to-skull mappings.

papers.title: Sleep neurophysiology as a biological correlate of infant temperament.
papers.abstract: Temperament, characterized as individual differences in reactivity and self-regulation, influences our behavior in everyday situations. It is apparent as early as infancy and shaped by genetic and environmental factors. A neurophysiological marker of temperament has been quantified during the waking state; however, it remains unknown how these associations manifest in sleep. To address this gap, we assessed nighttime sleep in 29 6-month-old infants (Mage = 6.145 months, SD = 0.399, 48% males) using a portable high-density electroencephalography. Temperament was assessed using a parent-rated questionnaire, focusing on 2 scales: negative affectivity and orienting/regulatory capacity. The correlation analyses included: (i) frontal asymmetry and (ii) whole-brain, electrode-wise correlations with temperament. The predefined frontal asymmetry correlation revealed that increased left-hemispheric slow-wave activity (SWA) corresponded to higher orienting/regulatory capacity scores. The whole-brain correlation showed that higher theta power across an array of electrodes over the prefrontal regions was associated with decreased negative affectivity scores. Local sleep depth over frontal and temporal brain areas, as reflected by SWA asymmetry and theta power, serves as a marker of self-regulatory abilities and affective traits, which, in turn, reflect differences in temperament. Our findings reveal that sleep neurophysiology is a biological correlate of temperament during preverbal stages.

papers.title: Sleep-dependent DNA methylation remodeling in basolateral amygdala fear engrams.
papers.abstract: How sleep consolidates fear memories at the molecular level within individual engram neurons is unknown. Using activity-dependent tagging and sequencing, we profiled the DNA methylome and transcriptome of engram and non-engram nuclei from the basolateral amygdala (BLA) after contextual fear conditioning with and without post-learning sleep deprivation. Fear learning induces coordinated CpG and CpH DNA methylation remodeling specifically in engram neurons, with each showing unique temporal dynamics, revealing CpH methylation as a separate component of the engram's epigenetic signature. Interestingly, sleep deprivation partially reverses learning-induced methylation changes and impairs memory recall, indicating that sleep supports engram-specific epigenetic consolidation. Integrating the engram methylome with single-cell transcriptome profiling, we construct a multi-omic molecular atlas of the BLA fear engram and identify Mid1 as a learning- and sleep-regulated methylation target. BLA-wide and engram-specific Mid1 knockdown establishes its functional requirement for fear memory consolidation, providing an approach to identify behaviorally relevant epigenetic targets.

papers.title: The role of BDNF, CREB, DAT, GFAP and Arc in manic- and OCD-like behavioral phenotypes in both sexes of rats exposed to REM sleep deprivation.
papers.abstract: Rapid-eye movement sleep deprivation (REM SD) has controversial effects on behavioral functions and cognitive abilities. Recent evidence has shown that REM SD in rats may lead to manic- and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)-like behaviors. The present study aimed to assess the effect of REM SD in both sexes of rats on locomotor activity, anxiety-like behavior, stereotyped behaviors, and OCD-like behavior. The possible role of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), cAMP response element-binding (CREB), dopamine transporter (DAT), glia fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), and activity-regulated cytoskeleton-associated protein (Arc) was also assessed using real-time PCR. REM SD was done for 14 days (6 h/d). Locomotor activity, anxiety-like behavior, grooming, and sniffing were measured using the open field test, and the marble burying test measured repetitive/compulsive-like responses. The results showed REM SD in both sexes led to hyperlocomotion, decreased anxiety, and increased OCD-like and stereotyped behaviors, with more effects in females except anxiety-like behavior. Also, the expression level of BDNF, CREB, DAT, and Arc was decreased and GFAP was increased in the hippocampus of both sexes of REM SD rats, with more effects in females except CREB. In conclusion, and for the first time, the present study showed the possible role of Arc, DAT, and GFAP in the induction of OCD- and manic-like behaviors and stereotyped behaviors in both sexes of rats. We also observed reduced BDNF and CREB expression in REM SD animals, suggesting a potential association between these molecular alterations and the behavioral changes induced by REM SD. Interventions targeting these molecular pathways could offer promising therapeutic strategies for REM SD-induced mood disorders.

papers.title: Cross-Domain Slow Wave Sleep Detection from Single-Lead EEG in Pediatric Congenital Heart Disease Recovery.
papers.abstract: Slow wave sleep (SWS) is vital for neural recovery and cardiovascular stability in children following congenital heart disease (CHD) surgery. However, pediatric CHD sleep patterns are often disrupted by clinical stressors and exhibit substantial domain discrepancies relative to adult data distributions. To address these challenges, this study establishes the Pediatric Cardiac Post-surgical Sleep (PCPS) dataset, a self-collected and expert-annotated pediatric polysomnography (PSG) dataset specifically targeting the early post-CHD surgical period. We further propose PCPS-SleepNet, an end-to-end deep learning framework for cross-domain sleep staging from single-lead EEG, enabling effective knowledge transfer from public sleep data to pediatric post-surgical CHD data. The architecture employs a multi-band input representation across six sub-bands and leverages a Four-Stage Progressive Encoder integrating Multi-Scale Depthwise Convolution (MSDC) for local features, self-attention for global density modeling, and a Conformer block for hybrid refinement. To mitigate limited pediatric data availability and domain shift, this network is pre-trained on public datasets and fine-tuned on the PCPS dataset. Subject-independent validation showed competitive performance, with an overall accuracy of 75.65 ± 0.58%, an AUROC of 89.06 ± 0.18%, an AUPRC of 83.49 ± 0.13%, and a macro F1-score of 76.68 ± 0.70%. For SWS detection, the model achieved an AUPRC of 87.89 ± 0.20% and an F1-score of 81.55 ± 0.74%. Architectural ablations and frequency-band input contribution analysis supported the model design and suggested the complementary discriminative value of slow-wave frequency-band inputs. These results suggest a practical and patient-friendly sleep detection solution for individualized sleep assessment and rehabilitation in vulnerable pediatric populations.

papers.title: An EEG-fMRI Jointly Constrained Digital Twin Brain and Its Application in Alzheime's Disease
papers.abstract: Current digital twin brain (DTB) models are typically optimized using single-modality functional neuroimaging data, which restricts their ability to simulate brain dynamics across multiple spatiotemporal scales. Here, we show that a two-stage DTB (TS-DTB) modeling framework jointly constrained by functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and electroencephalography (EEG) data. Validation in both the healthy young and Alzheimer's disease (AD) cohorts demonstrates that the TS-DTB model simultaneously captures subject-specific features of multi-scale brain dynamics. In particular, the TS-DTB models of AD patients successfully recapitulate spectral-temporal signatures of cognitive decline, suggesting a model-inferred association between these deficits and simulated excitation-inhibition (E-I) imbalances. By simulating responses to repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), we further reveal that acute EEG normalization in AD patients is computationally associated with putative E-I rebalancing via model-inferred synaptic reconfiguration and background suppression. Overall, these findings underscore the potential of the TS-DTB to advance the mechanistic understanding of the brain and inform personalized digital therapeutics.

papers.title: Sequential Associations of Sleep Architecture, Nocturnal Oxygenation, and Respiratory Disturbance With a Composite PSG-Derived Rhythm-Event Index.
papers.abstract: Sleep-disordered breathing (SDB), particularly obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), has been associated with cardiovascular complications including cardiac arrhythmias. However, the relative contributions of respiratory, oxygenation, and sleep architecture indices to composite PSG-derived rhythm-event index remain incompletely understood. To investigate the sequential associations of sleep architecture, nocturnal oxygenation, and respiratory disturbance indices with the composite PSG-derived rhythm-event index in patients undergoing polysomnography (PSG). Demographic, respiratory, oxygenation and sleep-architecture variables were extracted from PSG records. The primary outcome was a composite PSG-derived rhythm-event count, estimated as round(arrhythmia index × TST_hours) from the PSG-exported arrhythmia index, which was calculated during total sleep time only. Negative binomial regression used an offset of log(TST_hours). Because the outcome demonstrated overdispersion, negative binomial regression with an offset of log(TST hours) was used. Because the original 14-predictor model was over-parameterized for the sample size, a six-predictor model (age, sex, BMI, AHI, T90, and sleep efficiency) was chosen post hoc. This reduced model was not prespecified before the original analysis. Sleep efficiency was retained because it showed a strong signal in the exploratory 14-predictor model. The resulting p-values should therefore be interpreted as optimistic and exploratory. A sequential model-building approach (Model 1: age, sex, BMI, AHI; Model 2: plus T90; Model 3: plus sleep efficiency) was used to document the incremental contribution of each domain. A fully adjusted 14-predictor model was fitted only as a supplementary analysis. Wald 95% CIs and bootstrap percentile 95% CIs (2000 resamples) are reported. Forty-one participants were included (mean age 47.8 ± 13.5 years; median BMI 29.4 kg/m2). Severe OSA (AHI ≥ 30 events/hour) was present in 56.1%. Median arrhythmia index was 3.2 events/hour, with marked overdispersion. In the six-predictor model, only higher sleep efficiency was associated with lower arrhythmia rate (IRR = 0.946 per 1 percentage-point increase, 95% CI 0.921-0.972, p < 0.001; bootstrap 95% CI 0.888-0.984). T90 was associated in the Wald inference (IRR = 1.034, 95% CI 1.006-1.063, p = 0.016) but this association was not robust under bootstrap resampling (95% CI 0.979-1.067). AHI was not associated with arrhythmia rate (IRR = 1.000, 95% CI 0.987-1.014, p = 0.954). Age, sex and BMI were also not significant. A 14-predictor exploratory model had a marginally lower AIC (411.4) but a substantially higher BIC (438.8), consistent with overfitting. In this exploratory selected sleep-center cohort, AHI and other respiratory-event indices were not independently associated with the composite PSG-derived rhythm-event index. Only higher sleep efficiency showed a robust association with lower arrhythmia rate, but this finding is hypothesis-generating and may reflect unmeasured confounding. These results require confirmation in larger prospective studies and should not guide clinical risk stratification.

papers.title: Learning discriminative time-frequency representations for EEG segment-level seizure-state classification with channel selection.
papers.abstract: AbstractElectroencephalography (EEG)-based seizure monitoring supports the diagnosis andmanagement of epilepsy; however, high-dimensional multichannel EEG recordings imposesubstantial computational burden and limit suitability for portable monitoring systems.This paper proposes a reduced-channel framework for segment-level classification of EEGinto ictal, preictal and interictal states. It integrates attention-guided EEG channelselection, high-resolution time-frequency analysis via the Time ReassignedMultiSynchroSqueezing Transform (TMSST) and Concentration of Frequency and Time(ConceFT), and a hybrid CNN-BiLSTM classifier. The framework is evaluated on theCHB-MIT and Siena Scalp EEG databases under two complementary protocols: astratified 70/30 holdout split and rigorous Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) cross-validationto assess subject independent generalization. Under holdout evaluation using a single EEGchannel, the proposed framework achieves an accuracy of 99.28 ± 0.63%, sensitivity of99.18%, specificity of 99.64%, and MCC of 0.97 on CHB-MIT, and an accuracy of98.75 ± 0.74%, sensitivity of 98.77%, specificity of 99.38%, and MCC(Matthews correlationcoefficients) of 0.97 on Siena. LOSO cross-validation demonstrates subject independentgeneralization, exceeding 91% accuracy on both databases. These results demonstrate thatthe framework achieves an effective balance among segment-level classification accuracy,computational efficiency and reduced-channel operation. Moreover, applicability forportable and wearable EEG-based seizure-state monitoring applications is investigated.

papers.title: Interictal epileptic discharge > 1% associated with cognitive impairment in adult patients with epilepsy: A cross-sectional study based on dose-response relationship and discharge characteristics.
papers.abstract: Epilepsy is frequently accompanied by multidomain cognitive impairment, but the quantitative contribution of interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs)-including discharge burden, vigilance state, and spatial distribution-to specific cognitive domains remains incompletely defined. This cross-sectional study aimed to examine associations between multidimensional IED parameters and domain-specific cognitive function in non-symptomatic adult epilepsy. We analyzed long-term EEG-derived IED indices during sleep and wakefulness, lateralization, focal/multifocal distribution, and frontal/temporal involvement in 114 adults with non-symptomatic epilepsy, relating these metrics to a neuropsychological battery using ANCOVA with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. After adjustment for age, education, disease duration, seizure duration, seizure frequency, and antiepileptic drug count, a sleep IED index > 1% remained associated with lower Montreal Cognitive Assessment, associative learning, and verbal fluency scores versus the < 1% group; Mini-Mental State Examination was borderline and visual recognition did not survive FDR. Compared with no discharge, sleep > 1% showed lower Digit Symbol and verbal fluency scores only at uncorrected significance. For wakefulness, no significant graded association emerged between < 1% and > 1% groups; versus no discharge, wake > 1% showed lower Digit Symbol and verbal fluency scores at uncorrected level only. Discharges during both sleep and wakefulness were associated with lower backward digit span than sleep-only discharges, with a trend after FDR. Lateralization and focal/multifocal distribution were not significantly associated after FDR. Frontal IEDs were associated with lower verbal fluency and attention-related scores versus no discharge, but direct regional contrasts were nonsignificant and limited by small subgroups. A sleep IED index > 1% may represent a candidate electrophysiological marker of domain-specific cognitive vulnerability, whereas a wakefulness threshold and clear regional specificity were not definitively established. These findings support vigilance-state-aware quantification of IED burden while highlighting the need for larger longitudinal studies with detailed medication profiling.

papers.title: A representation-level wavelet-EMD fusion framework for spectral analysis and detection of epileptiform patterns in pediatric EEG: computational validation with a roadmap for external benchmarking.
papers.abstract: Pediatric EEG analysis for epilepsy detection is challenged by the non-stationary and developmentally heterogeneous nature of epileptiform activity. Conventional Fourier approaches provide limited time-frequency localization, whereas single-domain methods such as the wavelet transform and empirical mode decomposition (EMD) each exhibit complementary weaknesses. We developed a representation-level wavelet-EMD fusion framework that integrates wavelet and EMD spectra before feature extraction. The pipeline included adaptive wavelet denoising, energy-criterion EMD, weighted time-frequency fusion, extraction of eight spectral-temporal features, and classification using a soft-voting ensemble of a radial basis function support vector machine, random forest, and neural network. Evaluation was performed on 2,000 synthetic pediatric EEG segments spanning canonical epileptiform morphologies and multiple signal-to-noise ratios. A feature-level fusion variant was implemented as an ablation comparator to isolate the effect of fusion strategy while preserving identical feature extraction, classifier architecture, and validation procedures. Across 10-fold stratified cross-validation with 100 Monte Carlo replications, the proposed framework achieved 94.6 ± 0.6% accuracy, 93.7 ± 0.8% sensitivity, 95.5 ± 0.5% specificity, F1 score of 0.943 ± 0.007, and AUROC of 0.971 (95% CI, 0.962-0.978). Performance exceeded standalone wavelet, EMD, and Fourier baselines (all p < 0.001). Representation-level fusion also outperformed feature-level fusion by 1.4 percentage points in accuracy, with the greatest gains observed for polyspike and slow-wave morphologies. On the synthetic corpus the framework was competitive with EEGNet and a 1D convolutional network while retaining explicit time-frequency interpretability. In an external feasibility validation on the CHB-MIT pediatric scalp EEG corpus (14 subjects, leave-one-subject-out), representation-level fusion attained the highest performance of all methods (AUROC 0.901, accuracy 86.7%), confirming that the fusion strategy transfers to real recordings, with performance decreasing as expected. Representation-level wavelet-EMD fusion provides an interpretable and transparent computational framework for analyzing non-stationary pediatric epileptiform EEG whose advantage over classical time-frequency baselines persists, at feasibility scale, on real CHB-MIT recordings and remains competitive with deep-learning baselines. Because the primary evaluation is synthetic and the external validation is a feasibility-scale demonstration, these figures should be read as evidence of methodological viability and external transportability rather than definitive clinical performance; validation on larger, multi-center and prospective pediatric cohorts is the essential next step.

papers.title: Computational approaches to deep learning-driven EEG analysis for neurological disease diagnosis: a systematic review.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a widely used non-invasive neurophysiological technique for analyzing brain dynamics and diagnosing neurological diseases. However, the non-stationary nature, low signal-to-noise ratio, and inter-subject variability of EEG signals cause significant challenges to traditional analytical approaches. In recent years, deep learning has emerged as a powerful computational tool for EEG analysis, which enables automated feature learning and improved diagnostic accuracy with minimal human-driven feature extraction. This review systematically explains computational approaches in deep learning-driven EEG analysis for the diagnosis of neurological diseases. It includes recent advances in deep learning architectures, such as convolutional neural networks (CNN), recurrent neural networks (RNN), hybrid configurations, Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN), Large Language Models (LLM), autoencoders, and transformer-based models, with a focus on their capacity to model spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal dynamics in EEG signals. This is applicable in diagnosing major neurological disorders such as Epilepsy, Alzheimer's disease (AD), Encephalopathy, Parkinson's disease (PD), Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), sleep disorders, and developmental brain disorders. Furthermore, we discuss essential preprocessing strategies and denoising techniques, showing how removing biological artifacts prevents diagnostic models from confusing noise with actual signs of disease. Key challenges such as limited data availability, lack of model interpretability, inter-subject variability, and difficulty in clinical translation are identified and critically discussed. Finally, key emerging trends and future research directions are identified to support the development of clinical applications of EEG-based disease diagnostic systems.

papers.title: Algorithmic loops and the developing brain: a narrative review of dopaminergic mechanisms, sleep disruption, and neuroplasticity.
papers.abstract: Generation Alpha (born ~2010-2024) is the first cohort whose critical windows of dopaminergic maturation overlap entirely with mass exposure to AI-optimised short-form looping video platforms. Despite a robust epidemiological signal linking social media to depression, anxiety, attention deficits, and sleep disruption in youth, direct causal neurobiological data remain absent. This narrative review synthesises evidence from developmental neuroscience, mesolimbic dopamine physiology, sleep medicine, and longitudinal neuroimaging cohorts to articulate a mechanistic framework: chronic exposure to algorithmically engineered variable ratio reinforcement schedules may produce homeostatic D2/D3 receptor downregulation in the developing striatum, functionally analogous to the neuroadaptations observed in substance use disorders. This deficit state, characterised by anhedonia and acquired attentional dysregulation, is plausibly amplified by algorithmic disruption of slow-wave sleep-the biological window for glymphatic metabolite clearance and synaptic homeostasis. Converging evidence from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study documents associations between screen behaviour and grey matter volume, reward-circuit activation, and executive function trajectories across early adolescence. Because direct in vivo measurement of D2 receptor density in children using PET radioligands is ethically prohibited, we propose a cross-species, multimodal longitudinal research framework. This integrates a novel nonhuman primate digital self-administration paradigm with human cohort studies utilising computational phenotyping of algorithmic dosage, polysomnographic sleep monitoring, and annual reward-task fMRI. Current evidence justifies both urgent regulatory action and a dedicated research programme to characterise the neurobiological consequences of a uniquely 21st-century exposure.

papers.title: Rest-activity rhythm robustness and prospective mood symptoms in adolescence: Moderating effects of chronotype, sleep timing, and reward sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Adolescence is a period of heightened bipolar spectrum disorder (BSD) risk involving changes in reward and circadian systems. Circadian disruptions can destabilize mood, and the impact may be more pronounced in individuals with trait vulnerabilities. We tested whether greater reward sensitivity or eveningness influenced the predictive association between rest-activity rhythm (RAR) disruption and dimensional mood symptoms relevant to BSD. Adolescents (N = 199) in a prospective BSD-risk study completed baseline measures of reward sensitivity, morningness-eveningness, mood symptoms, and one week of actigraphy to generate Circadian Function Index (CFI), a composite measure of RAR robustness. Mood measures were readministered six months later. Regression models tested interactions between reward sensitivity, morningness-eveningness, and sleep midpoint and CFI to predict hypo-/manic or depressive symptom severity at follow-up. CFI was not independently associated with mood symptoms. Morningness-eveningness (b = 0.59, p < .001) and sleep midpoint (b = -2.77, p = .013) significantly moderated the association between CFI and hypo-/manic symptoms. Sleep midpoint (b = -5.40, p = .023) and reward sensitivity (b = -1.32, p = .033) significantly moderated the association between CFI and depressive symptoms. The impact of CFI on mood symptoms depended upon vulnerabilities. Lower CFI predicted greater hypo-/manic symptoms among adolescents with greater eveningness and later sleep midpoint. Lower CFI predicted greater depressive symptoms among those with later sleep midpoint. Contrary to hypotheses, higher CFI predicted greater depressive symptoms for adolescents with reward hyposensitivity. These results highlight potential targets for future identification studies relevant to BSD.

papers.title: Combined vitamins C and E attenuate memory impairment and hippocampal damage in diabetic sleep-deprived mice: behavioral and molecular insights.
papers.abstract: Diabetes mellitus (DM) and sleep disturbances are associated with cognitive impairment and hippocampal dysfunction, potentially involving oxidative stress and neuroinflammation. This study investigated the effects of vitamins C and E, individually and in combination, to determine whether their complementary antioxidant properties provide enhanced neuroprotective effects against cognitive and hippocampal alterations in diabetic sleep-deprived mice. Diabetes was induced in male BALB/c mice (25-30 g) by streptozotocin (60 mg/kg), followed by partial sleep deprivation using the inverted flowerpot method. Animals received vitamin C (50 mg/kg), vitamin E (100 mg/kg), or their combination for 20 days. Body weight and blood glucose were monitored. Spatial learning and memory were evaluated using the Morris water maze. Hippocampal histopathology, GFAP immunostaining, and expression of genes related to oxidative stress, inflammation, and neuroprotection were assessed. Vitamin E and combined vitamin C and E treatment reduced FBG and were associated with higher final body weight than untreated diabetic sleep-deprived mice. Vitamin treatments improved spatial learning and memory, with combined treatment producing greater improvements in selected behavioral outcomes. Combined treatment increased hippocampal neuronal density and reduced GFAP immunoreactivity. Vitamin treatment increased BDNF, Nrf2, and HO-1 expression and reduced iNOS, TNF-α, and IL-1β expression. Vitamin C and E, particularly in combination, were associated with improved metabolic, cognitive, and hippocampal outcomes in diabetic sleep-deprived mice, potentially involving modulation of neuroinflammatory and oxidative stress-related markers.

papers.title: A transient decrease in night-to-night variability of REM sleep before myocardial infarction
papers.abstract: Background. Myocardial infarction (MI) outcomes depend on time to treatment, and fatigue and sleep disturbance are often reported in the weeks before the event. Whether wearable-measured sleep changes within individuals before MI, and whether such change is specific to MI, is unknown. Methods. In the All of Us Research Program, adults with a first MI code and at least 180 valid Fitbit sleep nights in the preceding 360 days were matched to up to 10 controls on sex, comorbidities, sleep apnea, calendar time and a propensity score. The full matched cohort of all cases was the primary cohort, and cases with diabetes and/or hypertension formed a subgroup. The main endpoints were the within-person change in night-to-night variability (SD, RMSSD, CV) of the REM-sleep fraction at days 30-16 relative to each persons baseline (days 360-121) and from days 30-16 to days 15-1, tested against 10,000 randomly placed index dates with allowance for the choice of window (max-T). The same pipeline was applied to cases without recorded symptoms or treatment, to an index date at the first angina code, to a cohort including heart failure and to ischaemic stroke and admissions for heart failure, pneumonia, fracture or appendicitis and any cause, and the analysis was adjusted for nightly heart rate, wear and device. Results. The full matched cohort comprised 45 cases and 450 controls. REM-fraction variability changed transiently before MI, decreasing at days 30-16 and returning towards baseline over days 15-1; allowing for the choice of window, this decrease-then-return pattern was rarely matched at 10,000 randomly placed index dates (max-T p<0.001). Its components were the decrease in SD at days 30-16 (Cliffs {delta} -0.30, p=0.004; OR per SD 0.53, 95% CI 0.35-0.80; max-T p=0.0034) and the return in RMSSD over days 15-1 ({delta} +0.36, p<0.001; max-T p=0.0035); day by day, the decrease was not detected as a continuous change (cluster permutation test p=0.58). The decrease in SD was not seen at the same time before admissions for pneumonia (69 cases), fracture or appendicitis (130) or any cause (859) and was larger before MI than before each of them (difference in {delta} -0.25 to -0.34), whereas the rise over days 15-1 was shared with pneumonia; it was of similar size in the subgroup with diabetes and/or hypertension, in cases without recorded symptoms or treatment, with the index date at the first angina code, when people with heart failure were included and after adjustment for nightly heart rate, wear and device. Scoring each person against their own baseline discriminated cases from controls with AUCs of up to 0.66, probably an optimistic estimate because the decrease in RMSSD was attenuated in held-out halves of the matched sets. Conclusions. In adults who use consumer wearables, a first MI was preceded by a transient change in night-to-night REM-sleep variability, a decrease at days 30-16 and a return over the following two weeks. The decrease was not seen at the same time before other acute admissions, did not depend on recorded symptoms or treatment and was detectable against each persons own baseline with simple measures. The timing is an exploratory finding, to be confirmed in new cases.

papers.title: Sleep Strategies and Performance Outcomes in Ultramarathon Runners: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Ultramarathon events impose prolonged physiological and cognitive demands, often spanning 1 or more nights with limited sleep opportunity. To examine associations between pre-race and intra-race sleep strategies and physical and cognitive performance outcomes in ultramarathon runners. PubMed, EMBASE, PsycINFO, SPORTDiscus, and Web of Science were searched from inception to July 25, 2025. Primary observational or experimental studies published in English, or available in English translation were eligible when they involved ultramarathon runners (>42.2 km) and reported sleep as a variable of interest in relation to race performance or cognitive performance. Systematic review. Level 3. Two reviewers independently extracted study design, participant characteristics, race characteristics, sleep outcomes, performance outcomes, and cognitive outcomes. Methodological quality was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal checklists. Nine studies involving 2262 participants were included, with overall low risk of bias. Of the 4 studies examining pre-race sleep, 3 reported a significant association or group difference with a race-performance outcome. Reduced sleep was generally associated with poorer physical and cognitive performance. Greater intra-race sleep duration was consistently associated with longer finish times, reflecting additional nonmoving time and increased sleep need in longer events. Greater pre-race sleep duration, including sleep extension, was associated with faster finish times, and better pre-race sleep quality was linked to higher cognitive performance. Pre-race sleep extension was associated with faster finish times, although the observational evidence does not establish causality. Further research using objective sleep measures and controlled designs is required.

papers.title: Interactions between sleep parameters and heart rate variability in temporomandibular disorders.
papers.abstract: Temporomandibular disorders (TMD) cause pain and dysfunction in the temporomandibular joints (TMJs) and masticatory muscles and significantly impact quality of life. Temporomandibular disorderrelated pain is associated with sleep disorders and affects heart rate (HR) parameters; however, data from polysomnographic studies remains inconclusive. The aim of the study was to evaluate the impact of TMD on sleep parameters recorded using video-polysomnography (vPSG) and heart rate variability (HRV) monitored with the use of a 24-hour electrocardiogram (ECG). A cross-sectional study included 93 patients with TMD diagnosed according to the Diagnostic Criteria for Temporomandibular Disorders (DC/TMD). Video-polysomnography and 24-hour ECG monitoring were conducted. Pain was assessed using the numeric rating scale (NRS) (0-10) and categorized as mild (≤5) or severe (>5). The study included 93 patients with TMD, divided into groups of low pain intensity (n = 66) and high pain intensity (n = 27). The group with high pain intensity demonstrated lower sleep efficiency (87.7% vs. 90.8%, p = 0.022) and lower oxygen saturation (94.7% vs. 95.2%, p = 0.036). Heart rate variability parameters were similar in both groups. Women reported a higher total pain score (20 vs. 10, p = 0.007) and had a higher percentage of normal-to-normal (NN) intervals differing by more than 50 ms (pNN50) (24 h: 22.5% vs. 14.2%, p = 0.013; daytime: 18.0% vs. 9.8%, p = 0.002), higher daytime root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD) (41.7 vs. 34.8, p = 0.026), and a higher nighttime HR (63.8 vs. 60.5, p = 0.047). Additionally, women demonstrated lower values for very low frequency (VLF) power (1,402.4 vs. 2,214.5, p = 0.010), low frequency (LF) power (1,415.5 vs. 2,494.5, p = 0.028), and the low frequency/high frequency (LF/HF) ratio (1.3 vs. 2.5, p < 0.001). High TMD-related pain intensity is associated with reduced sleep efficiency and lower mean oxygen saturation during sleep. Women experience higher pain intensity but lower sympathetic activation than men.

papers.title: The toll of an early bell? School start time and adolescent sleep quality in Flanders, Belgium
papers.abstract: Study objectives: Adolescent sleep deprivation is a major public health concern, with insufficient and poor-quality sleep associated with adverse physical, mental and cognitive outcomes. Early school start times may contribute to sleep restriction by conflicting with the biologically delayed sleep patterns that emerge during puberty. This study examined the effect of school start times on sleep duration and sleep quality among secondary school students. Methods: Data were obtained from the 2022 Flemish Health Behaviour in School-aged Children (HBSC) study, including 12,329 adolescents from grade 1 to 6 in 94 secondary schools in Flanders. School start times were obtained from participating schools and sleep duration and sleep quality were assessed using self-report measures. Data were analyzed using traditional statistical methods (i.e., linear regression) and debiased machine learning methods (i.e., assumption lean regression, dose response curves and modified treatment policies). Results: No clinically meaningful effects of school start times on sleep outcomes were observed. In machine learning models, a 10-minute delay in start time was associated with non-significant changes in sleep quality (0.01 points on a 1-5 scale; 95% CI, -0.05 to 0.06) and school-day sleep duration (3.5 minutes; 95% CI, -1.0 to 8.0). Conclusions: Within the narrow range of school start times observed in Flemish secondary schools, confidence intervals excluded clinically meaningful effects of later start times on adolescent sleep duration and sleep quality. Whether larger delays would improve sleep remains to be determined.

papers.title: Using High-Performance Liquid Chromatography to Study Alterations in Biogenic Amines in Drosophila Models of Brain Disorders.
papers.abstract: Many neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders are characterized by disruptions in brain neurotransmitters, including alterations in the levels of the biogenic amines (BAs) dopamine (DA) and serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine; 5-HT), as well as in their release or reuptake. These neurochemical changes correlate with distinct key behavioral phenotypes, such as locomotor deficits, sleep fragmentation, and altered stress responses, among others. Because the principal BA systems interact, disease models frequently show coordinated shifts across multiple amines rather than isolated changes in a single neurotransmitter. Therefore, accurate, simultaneous quantification of several BAs is essential for interpreting behavioral and genetic findings. Drosophila melanogaster offers a genetically tractable system for modeling such disorders and neurotransmitter changes, but BAs occur in fly brain tissue at very low, nanomolar-to-femtomolar concentrations, and the small size of the Drosophila central nervous system makes their detection technically challenging. This study describes a protocol to detect and quantify DA, 5-HT, and octopamine in fly brains using high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with electrochemical detection (HPLC-ECD). HPLC-ECD was applied to detect changes in brain DA and 5-HT in a fly model of Parkinson's disease based on dopaminergic overexpression of human alpha-synuclein. Applying this protocol to the alpha-synuclein Parkinson's disease model reveals significantly elevated dopamine, but unchanged serotonin, relative to controls, consistent with early compensatory dopaminergic mechanisms. This approach provides a sensitive, low-cost, and readily accessible method for multiplexed BA quantification from limited Drosophila tissue. It also enables systematic screening of genetic modifiers and candidate therapeutics targeting monoaminergic pathways relevant to human brain disorders.

papers.title: Gene-by-Sleep Duration Interaction for Glycemic Traits in More Than 480,000 Individuals.
papers.abstract: The biological mechanisms of how sleep duration impacts type 2 diabetes pathogenesis and glycemic control are unclear. This study reveals 16 loci (11 novel) that interact with either short or long sleep duration to influence hemoglobin A1c, fasting glucose, or fasting insulin. Short and long sleep duration loci were nonoverlapping. Regulation of copper and diacylglycerol levels appear as distinct cellular mechanisms implicated by long and short sleep duration loci, respectively. Identified gene targets present insight for potential type 2 diabetes therapeutic design approaches related to JIP1-c-Jun N-terminal kinase interaction disruption, pericyte health, N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor activity, anti-inflammatory and leptin-enhancing dietary supplements, and serpins.

papers.title: Federated Spiking GANs with Rényi Differential Privacy for privacy-preserving synthetic EEG generation in brain-computer interfaces.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) data used in brain-computer and brain-machine interfaces (BCI/BMI) contain sensitive, user-specific information, creating privacy risks in consumer applications such as gaming, human augmentation, and virtual reality. Existing methods like encryption and anonymization either fail to protect data during analysis or still expose identifiable attributes. While differential privacy (DP) offers formal protection, it often reduces data utility. The key challenge is to generate synthetic EEG data that protects sensitive attributes while retaining temporal features for downstream use. To address this, we developed a federated spiking generative framework that integrates a spiking neural network (SNN)-based generator, temporally correlated noise, an artificial neural network (ANN)-based discriminator, and Rényi differential privacy (RDP) within a federated learning framework. The SNN-based generator captures temporal characteristics, and the ANN-based discriminator maintains classification accuracy. Federated training prevents centralization of raw client data, while privacy is preserved through controlled perturbation of spike-train and membrane-potential representations, supported by RDP-based privacy accounting. We evaluated our architecture against methods such as RDP-TimeGAN, RDP-CRNN-GAN, RDP-RCGAN, and RDP-Clare-GAN, demonstrating that our approach preserves temporal features and downstream utility while maintaining privacy in synthetic EEG generation. This solution enables privacy-preserving generation of distributed synthetic EEG data for BCI/BMI research and development.

papers.title: Theta-band EEG changes following sequential rTMS and tACS in fibromyalgia: A randomized controlled pilot study
papers.abstract: Background: Sequential application of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) and transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) may induce neurophysiological changes within sensorimotor and pain-related networks. However, the resting-state EEG effects of this combined approach in fibromyalgia remain unknown. Methods: In this exploratory randomized controlled pilot study, 10 adults with fibromyalgia were assigned to active stimulation (n = 5) or a no-stimulation control group (n = 5). Active participants received one or two sessions of 10-Hz rTMS over the left primary motor cortex (1,000 pulses/session), followed by 10 daily sessions of bilateral 10-Hz tACS (1 mA, 20 min). Six-minute eyes-closed resting-state EEG recordings were obtained before and after the intervention or an equivalent control interval. Power spectral density was quantified in the delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands and analyzed using mixed repeated-measures ANOVAs across central-centroparietal and posterior regions of interest. Results: Theta power increased significantly in the active group but not in controls, yielding significant Time x Group (F(1,8)=8.70, p=.018, p2=.521) and Time x ROI x Group (F(1,8)=5.53, p=.047, p2=.409) interactions. Follow-up analyses showed increased theta power in both central-centroparietal (p=.004) and posterior (p=.012) regions, with a larger increase observed posteriorly. No significant interaction effects were found for delta, alpha, or beta power. Conclusions: Sequential motor-cortex rTMS followed by repeated bilateral 10-Hz tACS was associated with increased resting-state theta activity in fibromyalgia. Given the small sample size, post hoc ROI selection, lack of sham stimulation, and absence of component-specific control conditions, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and require replication in adequately powered sham-controlled studies.

papers.title: Who's Been Sleeping in My Bedroom? Associations Between Co-Sleeping with Dogs, Cats, or Children and Sleep and Cardiorespiratory Physiology Among WHOOP Users.
papers.abstract: Co-sleeping with pets or children is common, yet its associations with sleep, cardiorespiratory physiology, and behavioral outcomes are understudied. We examined within-person associations between co-sleeping with a dog, cat, or child and sleep characteristics, measures of cardiorespiratory physiology, and next-day physical activity. We analyzed 1,649,083 person-days from 11,733 adults wearing the WHOOP wearable device. Participants self-reported nightly co-sleeping via a daily journal in the device's companion smartphone application. Linear mixed-effects models compared nights with and without co-sleeping within the same individual. Co-sleeping was associated with lower resting heart rate (0.8-1.1 beats/min), lower respiratory rate (0.04-0.07 breaths/min), and higher heart rate variability (1.41-1.95 ms). Sleep outcomes were mixed, with longer sleep duration (5.5-9.6 min) but more disturbances (0.36-0.40 instances) and slightly less restorative sleep (0.23-1.17%). Associations were generally consistent across groups, although child co-sleeping was associated with greater sleep disruption. Next-day physical activity was higher following dog and cat co-sleeping (7.6 and 7.4 intensity-weighted min, respectively) but lower following child co-sleeping (-2.6 intensity-weighted min). Despite statistical significance, all standardized effect sizes were small (β range: 0.008-0.045). Co-sleeping was associated with small differences in cardiorespiratory physiology (lower resting heart rate, higher heart rate variability) alongside mildly greater sleep disruption. The small magnitude of these associations suggests that co-sleeping decisions may be influenced more by personal and contextual factors than by expectations of substantive physiologic or sleep-related impacts.

Respiratory rate was higher (53.2 ± 9.1 vs. 49.6 ± 9.5 breaths/min), but not significant after correction (adjusted p = 0.126). papers.title: Electroacupuncture improves endometrial receptivity and pregnancy outcomes in controlled ovarian hyperstimulation rats by restoring Per2 circadian rhythm.
papers.abstract: Controlled ovarian hyperstimulation (COH) is a critical step in in vitro fertilization-embryo transfer (IVF-ET). However, the decline in endometrial receptivity caused by COH severely restricts the success rate of implantation. Previous studies mostly focused on static molecular events, lacking a systematic exploration from the perspective of dynamic rhythms. This study aims to explore whether electroacupuncture (EA) can improve endometrial receptivity and pregnancy outcomes by repairing the disordered rhythm of the core clock gene Per2 in the endometrium caused by COH from the perspective of chronobiology. A COH model was established using 126 Sprague - Dawley (SD) rats. Following EA intervention, dynamic sampling was conducted during the implantation window to assess clock gene rhythmicity, the expression of receptivity - related factors, and uterine morphological changes. Per2-/- mice were used to preliminarily investigate whether Per2 participates in mediating the effects of EA. COH induced an abnormal increase in serum progesterone, leading to desynchronization of the endometrial clock gene network. Among them, the peak delay of the core clock gene Per2 was highly coupled with the abnormal peak of progesterone in time, and presented an anti - phase oscillatory pattern with the expression of the angiogenesis factor Vegf. During the implantation window, the expression of Vegf and integrin αvβ3 was down - regulated, the development of pinopodes degenerated, and the pregnancy rate was significantly reduced. EA could correct the abnormal progesterone level, repair the rhythm parameters of Per2, up - regulate the expression of Vegf and integrin αvβ3, improve the development of pinopodes, and significantly increase the pregnancy rate. In Per2-/- mice, the up - regulating effect of EA on Vegf and Integrin αvβ3 was significantly weakened, preliminarily suggesting that Per2 may participate in mediating the effects of EA on endometrial receptivity. This study provided preliminary evidence for a novel mechanism by which COH impairs endometrial receptivity from the perspective of dynamic circadian rhythm, providing experimental evidence for EA as an adjuvant intervention strategy based on circadian clock regulation in IVF-ET cycles.

papers.title: Strategies to establish a biologically defined Parkinson's disease cohort prior to the onset of clinically significant motor symptoms
papers.abstract: Identifying individuals at risk for neurodegeneration is a priority for clinical trials. Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI) deploys strategies to enroll individuals before typical clinical Parkinson's disease symptoms: recruiting polysomnogram-confirmed REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) and central identification of hyposmia via smell testing. Groups were divided into RBD with and without hyposmia (RBD+Hyposmia, RBD-Hyposmia) and hyposmia with and without self-reported dream enactment behavior (Hyposmia+DEB, Hyposmia-DEB). Participants underwent clinical and biomarker testing including CSF alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay (CSFaSynSAA) and dopamine transporter imaging. While all enrollment strategies showed robust enrichment for CSFaSynSAA positivity, RBD+Hyposmia and Hyposmia+DEB were more likely CSFaSynSAA+ (94% and 85%) vs RBD-Hyposmia (40%) and Hyposmia-DEB (55%). Among CSFaSynSAA+, RBD+Hyposmia and Hyposmia+DEB had more mood, autonomic, and cognitive symptoms than Hyposmia-DEB. PPMI identified a large biologically-defined early neuronal synucleinopathy cohort and demonstrated biomarker and multi-domain clinical heterogeneity within CSFaSynSAA+ individuals prior to symptom onset.

papers.title: Molecular mechanisms of YZG-331 ameliorated insomnia based on the gut microbiota-drug interaction.
papers.abstract: The gut microbiota plays a crucial role in the study of drug efficacy and metabolism. YZG-331 exhibits significant sedative and hypnotic effects. However, the oral bioavailability of YZG-331 in female mice remains low at 27.7%, and it exhibits instability in the gut microbiota, undergoing rapid metabolism, with the intestinal hydrolytic metabolite M2 identified as the characteristic metabolite. Both the underlying mechanisms of YZG-331 therapeutic effects on insomnia and its enzyme-mediated metabolic pathways involving the gut microbiota remain incompletely elucidated. In this study, we found that YZG-331 regulated the tryptophan metabolism and 5-HT production pathways by the gut microbiota. Specifically, YZG-331 increased the abundance of Lactobacillus and Muribaculaceae in the gut, with Lactobacillus reuteri playing a critical role in both the metabolic processes of YZG-331 and the biosynthesis of tryptophan-derived metabolites. YZG-331 enhanced the activation of the tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) cofactor system, which subsequently promoted tryptophan hydroxylase (TPH) activity, thereby enhancing 5-HT production. Furthermore, YZG-331 and M2 increased intestinal butyric acid levels, thereby promoting sleep regulation and supporting the restoration of the intestinal barrier. Overall, our study provided the first evidence highlighting the crucial role of the gut microbiota in the therapeutic mechanism and metabolic processing of YZG-331 in the treatment of insomnia.

papers.title: Association Between Circadian Rhythm Sleep Disorder and Noninfectious Uveitis: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
papers.abstract: Circadian misalignment influences ocular immune homeostasis, inflammatory signaling, and blood-retinal barrier integrity, each implicated in the pathogenesis of noninfectious uveitis (NIU). Whether clinically diagnosed circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder (CRSD) is associated with incident NIU is unknown. This study examined that association in a large multicenter cohort. This retrospective cohort study used the TriNetX federated network. Adults with CRSD (ICD-10 G47.2) were compared with adults who underwent polysomnography without a sleep disorder. Patients with uveitis before the index date or with causes of infectious or secondary intraocular inflammation were excluded. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression estimated adjusted hazard ratios (aHR) for incident anterior and composite NIU, adjusting for demographics, systemic comorbidities, corticosteroid exposure, and prior ophthalmology encounters. Major depressive disorder and appendicitis served as positive and negative control outcomes. The CRSD cohort included 47 323 adults and the comparator cohort 22 241 adults. CRSD was independently associated with an increased hazard of incident anterior NIU (aHR, 1.70; 95% CI, 1.11-2.61) and composite NIU (aHR, 1.84; 95% CI, 1.21-2.79). Control outcomes performed as expected, with a strong association for major depressive disorder (aHR, 2.19; 95% CI, 2.10-2.29) and no association for appendicitis (aHR, 1.12; 95% CI, 0.87-1.45). Clinically diagnosed CRSD was independently associated with an increased risk of incident NIU. These findings support a potential role for circadian dysregulation in ocular inflammatory disease and warrant prospective confirmation.

papers.title: Assessment of the duration of continuous EEG monitoring in aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) can detect seizures and delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI) in patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH). Because a standard duration of continuous EEG monitoring to capture these complications has not been established in aSAH, we compared a standard 6- or 7-day cEEG monitoring protocol versus longer periods of monitoring. We performed a retrospective analysis of aSAH patients ≥18 years old grouped by standard monitoring protocol (6-7 days, group 1) and those with longer monitoring (>7 days, group 2). Clinical characteristics, EEG features, length of stay (LOS) and functional outcome were compared using univariate analyses. Multivariable analyses tested the association between the groups and vasospasm, DCI, LOS, and modified Rankin Scale (mRS). 19 patients met criteria for group 1 and 16 patients for group 2. We found no difference in EEG's detection of worsening abnormal EEG activity, vasospasm and DCI. ICU and hospital LOS in group 2 were nearly double that of group 1 (ICU: 25.5 (19.5-35) vs. 14 (11-21) days, p = 0.0003; hospital: 32.5 (29.5-48) vs. 18 (13-29) days, p = 0.003). Good outcome (mRS ≤2) at discharge and at 6 months was similar in both groups (21.1% vs. 0% and 56.3% vs. 46.2%). In multivariable analysis, EEG duration was independently associated with ICU and hospital LOS but not with vasospasm, DCI, and mRS at 6 months. Longer EEG monitoring correlated with significantly longer ICU and hospital LOS but not with vasospasm, DCI, and functional outcome at 6 months. Larger studies to confirm our findings are warranted.

papers.title: Sleep quality, circadian rhythm disruption, functioning, and treatment adherence in major depression: a cross-sectional exploratory study.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances and circadian rhythm disruption are highly prevalent in major depressive disorder (MDD) and may contribute to poorer functioning and reduced treatment adherence. However, few studies have examined sleep quality, biological rhythm disruption, functioning, and medication adherence concurrently in an outpatient depression sample. This study investigated the relationships among sleep quality, biological rhythm, functional status, medication adherence, and depression severity in patients diagnosed with depression. A descriptive, correlational cross-sectional study was conducted in the Adult Psychiatry Outpatient Clinic of Maltepe University Faculty of Medicine Hospital between 16 December 2024 and 15 March 2025. A total of 110 patients with a confirmed diagnosis of depression were included. Sleep quality was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), biological rhythm disruption using the Biological Rhythm Interview of Assessment in Neuropsychiatry (BRIAN), functional status using the Social Functioning Scale (SFS-T), medication adherence using the Medication Adherence Rating Scale (MARS), and depression severity using the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI). Pearson correlation analyses were used to examine associations among variables, and multiple linear regression analyses were conducted to identify independent factors associated with sleep quality. Sleep impairment was common: 46.4% of participants reported moderate sleep quality and 31.8% reported poor sleep quality. Mean PSQI score was 8.31 (SD = 4.21). Poorer sleep quality (higher PSQI scores) was moderately associated with lower social functioning (r = - 0.300, p < 0.01) and lower medication adherence (r = - 0.350, p < 0.01), and strongly associated with greater biological rhythm disruption (r = 0.621, p < 0.01). Sleep quality was also positively correlated with depression severity (r = 0.494, p < 0.01). Sleep impairment was common: 46.4% of participants reported moderate sleep quality and 31.8% reported poor sleep quality. Poorer sleep quality (higher PSQI scores) was moderately associated with lower social functioning (r = - 0.300, p < 0.01) and lower medication adherence (r = - 0.350, p < 0.01), and positively associated with biological rhythm disruption (r = 0.621, p < 0.01) and depressive symptom severity (r = 0.494, p < 0.01). In the multiple linear regression analysis, the overall model was statistically significant (R² = 0.429, p < 0.001), explaining 42.9% of the variance in sleep quality. After adjustment for the other variables, biological rhythm disruption remained the only independent predictor of sleep quality (β = 0.445, p < 0.001). In this outpatient depression sample, poor sleep quality was significantly associated with circadian rhythm disruption, reduced functioning, lower medication adherence, and greater depressive symptom severity. These findings support the clinical value of early sleep screening and integrated approaches that address sleep-circadian regulation alongside functional recovery, with possible benefits for treatment engagement in outpatient mental health care. papers.title: Systematic Review of the Literature on Associations Between Symptoms, Stress, Resilience, and Epigenetic Aging in Patients With Cancer.
papers.abstract: Cancer and its treatments can have long-term adverse effects that may accelerate aging and worsen symptom burden. The cognitive and behavioral strategies that patients utilize to adapt to their environment and respond to stress may influence inter-individual variability in aging and symptom burden. This systematic review summarizes the relationships between symptoms, stress, resilience, and epigenetic aging in oncology patients and identifies knowledge gaps. A search of relevant databases was done from January 2000 to May 2026. Studies were included that examined DNA methylation patterns to predict biological age using algorithms known as epigenetic clocks in adults with cancer. A qualitative synthesis of the quantitative studies is reported. Of the 10 studies included in this review, a total of nine different methods were used to predict epigenetic age. The most common methods were the Levine, Horvath, and Hannum clocks. Nine studies reported on associations between symptoms and epigenetic age acceleration; one study reported on an association between stress and epigenetic age acceleration; and one study reported on an association between resilience and epigenetic age acceleration. More longitudinal studies are needed to validate these findings and investigate variations by epigenetic age estimate, timing of assessment, cancer type, and stage of disease. Studies are needed to evaluate the role of stress and resilience in mediating/moderating the relationships between epigenetic age acceleration and symptoms in patients with cancer. A subset of patients with cancer who develop more severe fatigue, pain, sleep disturbance, peripheral motor neuropathy, cognitive, depressive, and/or anxiety symptoms may experience epigenetic age acceleration. This systematic review was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD42024545895).

papers.title: When a Seizure Reveals More Than a Hemorrhage: When to Suspect Cerebral Cavernous Malformations.
papers.abstract: Cerebral cavernous malformations (CCMs) are low-flow vascular malformations that may be asymptomatic or present with seizures, hemorrhage, headache, or focal neurological deficits. Most are sporadic and solitary, whereas familial CCMs are associated with multiple lesions and autosomal-dominant inheritance. Distinguishing between these forms is clinically relevant for long-term management. We present a 33-year-old woman who presented with generalized tonic-clonic seizures following sleep deprivation. Computed tomography (CT) initially suggested a left frontal intraparenchymal hemorrhage. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) subsequently revealed two left frontal Zabramski type II CCMs. Electroencephalography showed cortical dysfunction with paroxysmal activity and contralateral propagation. Antiseizure treatment with phenytoin was initiated and later supplemented with levetiracetam. The patient remained asymptomatic and was referred for tertiary evaluation. This case highlights the diagnostic limitations of CT and the importance of MRI for CCM characterization and detection of multiple lesions. The presence of two cavernomas and a potentially relevant family history raises suspicion for familial CCM, although these findings alone do not establish a hereditary diagnosis. Genetic evaluation and detailed family assessment should therefore be considered. Treatment should be individualized; conservative management is appropriate in selected stable patients, whereas microsurgery and stereotactic radiosurgery are reserved for specific clinical scenarios.

papers.title: The role and mechanism of endothelial cell-specific molecule-1 in respiratory diseases.
papers.abstract: Endothelial cell-specific molecule-1 (ESM1) is a soluble dermatan sulfate proteoglycan and is mainly expressed in pulmonary endothelial cells. It is reported that ESM1 plays an important role in promoting cell proliferation, such as metabolic reprogramming, and inhibiting autophagy. In addition, ESM1 exerts a dual regulatory effect on inflammation. However, the mechanism of the dual regulatory effect of ESM1 on inflammation remains unclear. Moreover, evidence suggests that ESM1 is involved in multiple signaling pathways, such as the EGFR/ESM1, EGFR/HER3-Akt/ANGPT2, HGF/c-MET, VEGF-A/ESM1, mTOR, and ZEB1/PI3K/AKT pathways. Increasing studies suggested that ESM1 is involved in various respiratory diseases, such as lung cancer, obstructive sleep apnea hypopnea syndrome (OSAHS), pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), and acute lung injury (ALI)/acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). In lung cancer, ESM1 promotes cancer cell proliferation through the EGFR, NF-κB, and HGF/c-MET signaling pathways. In OSAHS, ESM1 enhances inflammatory factor secretion and monocyte-endothelial cell adhesion through the HIF-1α/VEGF signaling pathway. In PAH, ESM1 may promote vascular remodeling and inflammation via a positive feedback loop with TNF-α. Conversely, in ALI/ARDS, ESM1 may inhibit leukocyte recruitment to reduce inflammation. However, the specific roles and mechanisms of ESM1 in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), asthma, and pneumonia need to be further explored. Accordingly, ESM1 may serve as a potential therapeutic target for various respiratory diseases.

papers.title: Multisystem Outcomes of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists Versus Active Comparators in Type 2 Diabetes: A Multicenter Target Trial Emulation.
papers.abstract: Multisystem effects of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) beyond cardiometabolic outcomes are incompletely characterized against active comparators in type 2 diabetes (T2D). We compared GLP-1RA with sulfonylureas (SUs), sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2is), and dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (DPP4is) in adults with T2D. In a multicenter target trial emulation across 5 University of California academic medical centers (2012-2025) using harmonized electronic health record data, adults with T2D newly initiating GLP-1RA, SU, SGLT2i, or DPP4i were propensity score-matched 1-to-1 within site via least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (>11 000 covariates), with up to 5-year follow-up. We screened 181 prespecified incident outcomes across 15 body systems, pooling hazard ratios by random-effects meta-analysis. Robustness required leave-one-medical-center-out stability, E-value ≥1.5, and false discovery rate-adjusted P < .10. Among 70 982 matched adults, 118 robust associations were identified (65 for reduced risk and 53 for increased risk). Risk reductions were most consistent for cardiovascular outcomes, including myocarditis/cardiomyopathy (summary hazard ratio, 0.38 [95% CI, 0.32-0.44] vs SGLT2i), acute myocardial infarction (0.53 [0.42-0.66]), heart failure (0.71 [0.58-0.88] vs DPP4i), and thromboembolism (0.69-0.72), and for nephritis/nephrosis (0.73 [0.67-0.79]), nutritional anemia (0.70-0.81), coagulation disorders (0.73-0.81), and tobacco-related disorders (0.60 [0.49-0.74]). Risk increases were found for musculoskeletal conditions (22 associations); osteoarthritis 1.48 (1.29-1.68), stress fractures 1.68 (1.15-2.47), diverticular disease (1.18-1.33), sleep-wake disorders (1.27-1.54), and menopausal disorders (1.32-1.52). Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist initiation was associated with reduced cardiovascular, renal, hematologic, and tobacco-related risk, consistent with outcome trials. Increased risks for musculoskeletal, gastrointestinal, and sleep-wake disorders warrant monitoring as the clinical use of GLP-1RAs continues to expand.

papers.title: Real-Time Electronic Patient-Reported Outcome Monitoring With Digital Triage and Care-Team Integration in Early Breast Cancer: ENABLE Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: Electronic patient-reported outcomes (ePROs) can support patient-centered oncology care, but in early breast cancer, it is unclear whether real-time ePRO-triggered triage adds benefit beyond lower-intensity app-based support and scheduled ePRO collection. We tested whether adding weekly ePRO screening, rule-based triage, and care-team escalation to app-based support improves health-related quality of life (HRQoL) during systemic therapy for early breast cancer. ENABLE was a multicenter, open-label, parallel-group randomized controlled trial at 2 German university hospitals. Adults with early (stage I-III) breast cancer initiating systemic therapy were randomized 1:1 to reactive patient-reported outcome assessment (RPA) or control. Both arms received the ENABLE app with educational and organizational support and scheduled HRQoL assessments at 6 fixed time points; only RPA received weekly EuroQol Visual Analogue Scale screening (trigger: score <50 or ≥10-point decline) followed by symptom assessment, digital triage, and care-team alerts. Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System-29 was analyzed as an 8-measure HRQoL end-point family (7 domains plus pain intensity); no single domain, composite score, or binary global success rule was prespecified. Group-by-visit mixed-effects models were fitted with Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate adjustment. The recruitment period was March 22, 2021, to September 8, 2023. Of 605 randomized patients, 487 entered the modified intention-to-treat analysis (RPA: n=242; control: n=245). End-of-treatment between-group differences (RPA minus control, T-score points, 95% CI, and adjusted P) were: fatigue -3.90 (95% CI -5.77 to -2.03; P=.004), social participation +2.84 (95% CI 1.18 to 4.49; P=.01), anxiety -2.10 (95% CI -3.65 to -0.55; P=.049), depression -1.95 (95% CI -3.25 to -0.65; P=.10), sleep disturbance -1.82 (95% CI -3.43 to -0.20; P=.051), pain interference -1.44 (95% CI -3.38 to 0.49; P=.18), physical function +1.33 (95% CI -0.22 to 2.88; P=.18), and pain intensity -0.26 (95% CI -0.73 to 0.21; P=.32; 0-10 scale). All T-score differences were below the 5-point minimally important difference (MID). Exploratory time-to-deterioration analyses favored RPA for fatigue (hazard ratio [HR] 0.69, 95% CI 0.54-0.89), social participation (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.59-0.97), and depression (HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.44-0.98). Of 209 monitored RPA patients, 160 (76.6%; 95% CI 70.4-81.8) triggered at least 1 alert. No intervention-related harms were identified. ENABLE tests real-time, rule-based ePRO triage with care-team escalation against an active digital comparator rather than usual care, isolating the response pathway itself; it extends this design from metastatic disease into early breast cancer and escalates to the care team rather than to the patient alone. Benefits were domain-specific and sub-MID, in anxiety, fatigue, and social participation, tempering the expectation of a global HRQoL effect. For practice, symptom-triggered triage is a supportive-care workflow tool worth embedding where alerts reach a team that acts and documents, not a stand-alone remedy for treatment-related morbidity.

papers.title: Participation in an integrated telemedicine and psychological counseling program and psychological outcomes in patients with HCC: a multicenter retrospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: To examine associations between cumulative participation in an integrated telemedicine and psychological counseling program and psychological outcomes in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). This retrospective cohort included 349 patients at two Chinese hospitals during 2022-2023. Recorded cumulative completion defined low (< 50%), moderate (50-79%), and high (≥ 80%) participation. Twelve-month ANCOVA included 331 patients without recorded death, 50 imputations for nondeath missing outcomes, and 16-17 covariates and Benjamini-Hochberg correction across 18 contrasts. The service-recorded WHOQOL-BREF aggregate was exploratory because its scoring algorithm could not be verified. Progression-specific pattern-mixture analyses assessed missingness assumptions. Compared with low participation, moderate and high participation were associated with lower PHQ-9 scores (β = - 2.64; 95% CI - 3.36 to - 1.92 and - 3.73; - 4.49 to - 2.98, respectively), lower PSQI (β = - 1.99 and - 1.09) and distress scores (- 0.53 and - 0.87), and higher exploratory WHOQOL-BREF aggregates (4.69 and 3.45); all q < 0.05. High participation was also associated with lower GAD-7 (- 1.14; - 1.84 to - 0.43). Direct high-moderate comparisons favored high participation for depression and anxiety and moderate participation for sleep. FACT-Hep scores were lower with both moderate (- 8.70; - 11.68 to - 5.73) and high participation (- 8.93; - 12.31 to - 5.55). Participation showed outcome-specific associations, with more favorable psychological scores alongside poorer disease-specific quality of life. Clinical significance remains uncertain. Selection, residual confounding, cumulative exposure timing, and informative attrition limit interpretation; the findings do not establish an optimal participation level.
